title: Winning the Outpost
idea: Black has played e5 and a6, and in doing so has made a permanent hole on d5. A knight there would be untouchable — no pawn can ever attack it. But d5 is currently guarded by the knight on f6, so the plan is three moves long: trade off the defender, then occupy the square. Manoeuvring for a square rather than a piece is the thing that most separates a club player from a strong one.

cues.text: Black's pawns on e5 and a6 mean no black pawn can ever attack d5 or b5 again.
The only thing defending d5 is the knight on f6.
Your bishop on c1 can reach g5, where it attacks that defender.

recognition.prompt: Black has pawns on e5 and a6. What have those two moves cost him?

choices.why: With the e-pawn on e5 and the c-pawn long gone, no black pawn can ever attack d5. A knight there is safe forever, which is why the entire plan is about getting one to that square.

choices.text: The e5 pawn is weak and can be won
choices.why: It is defended and hard to attack. The square matters more than the pawn.
The king is fine. This is a structural weakness, not a tactical one.
They are useful moves, and they still cost a square permanently. Every pawn move does.

plan.goal: Trade off the knight on f6, because it is the only defender of d5.
Then put a knight on d5 and leave it there.
Do not push a pawn that would let Black challenge the square.

line.threat: Nothing hangs. There is a hole on d5 and one black piece defending it.
hints: You want a knight on d5. Something is stopping you.
Attack the defender rather than the square.
Bishop to g5, hitting the knight on f6.

moves.why: Attacks the only piece defending d5. You are not developing for its own sake — you are removing a guard.
Black contests d5 with a piece instead, which is the right idea but not enough.

hints: Carry out what Bg5 was for.
Remove the defender, even though it means giving up a bishop for a knight.

moves.why: Trading a bishop for a knight looks like a small concession and is not. In a position with a permanent hole, the knight that guards it is worth more than the bishop that removes it.
Black recaptures, and d5 is now defended only by the bishop on e6.

hints: The square is yours. Take it.

moves.why: The outpost is occupied. Black can trade the bishop for it, but then you simply recapture with a pawn and the square stays yours — and the knight cannot be driven off by anything.

terminal.summary: Three moves, one idea: find the square no pawn can ever attack, remove whatever defends it, and put a knight there. Nothing was captured for profit and no tactic was calculated. This is the manoeuvre to reach for when you look at a quiet position and do not know what to do — there is almost always a hole somewhere, and working out which of your pieces can get to it is a real plan.

moves.why: Solid development, but it does nothing about the knight on f6, so the outpost stays guarded.
Stops b5 and takes another square from Black. Useful, and slower than going straight for the plan.
